query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A high-temperature pre-oxidation treatment performed at approximately 1100°C for 1–2 hours in a low partial-pressure oxygen atmosphere (10⁻³–10⁻⁵ atm) will form a uniform, dense, and adherent protective oxide scale on refractory high‐entropy alloys, thereby significantly enhancing their high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to untreated alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy in its as-cast/homogenized state without any pre-formed protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: A single-step, high-temperature pre-oxidation treatment under controlled low oxygen partial pressure.
generation.conditions: Pre-oxidation at 1100°C for 1–2 hours in an oxygen atmosphere maintained at 10⁻³–10⁻⁵ atm, followed by cyclic oxidation exposure at 1200°C in air for 200 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a uniform, dense, and adherent oxide layer (such as a CrTaO₄-based scale or a mixed chromia/alumina oxide) on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The controlled pre-oxidation induces the development of a stable oxide scale that acts as an effective barrier to oxygen diffusion during subsequent high-temperature exposure, reducing further oxidation and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Pre-oxidized samples will exhibit a lower mass gain, improved oxide scale adhesion, and reduced oxygen penetration compared to untreated alloys when exposed to 1200°C cyclic oxidation in air for 200 hours.
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory HEA exposed directly to high-temperature oxidation conditions, resulting in higher mass gain, more extensive oxide spallation, and deeper oxygen penetration.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only for alloys that possess sufficient oxide‐forming elements and within the specified treatment parameters; deviations in oxygen partial pressure, temperature, or alloy composition may not yield the protective scale or the anticipated improvement.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the exact oxide composition and microstructural characteristics required for optimal protection, which may vary with specific alloy chemistries and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical refractory HEA specimens. Subject one set to the pre-oxidation treatment (1100°C, 1–2 hours, 10⁻³–10⁻⁵ atm O₂) and leave the other untreated. Then expose both sets to cyclic oxidation at 1200°C in air for 200 hours. Use thermogravimetric analysis, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) mapping to assess mass gain, oxide scale adhesion, and oxygen penetration depth.
measurements: Oxide scale adhesion and spallation (SEM/EDS qualitative assessment)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in mass gain, improved oxide scale adhesion (i.e., less spallation), and shallower oxygen penetration compared to untreated specimens, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ]. Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. decision.trend: Among refractory high-entropy alloys evaluated for extreme-temperature structural applications, three lines of work have directly addressed or at least mentioned oxidation behavior. First, researchers sought to incorporate in situ oxide- or carbide-forming elements (e.g., Al, Cr, Ti) into NbMoCrTiAl matrices, aiming to strengthen the alloys while maintaining some oxidation resistance, though actual high-temperature oxidation tests remained limited (PMC7513042). Second, studies of AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 under elevated-temperature wear conditions demonstrated that forming complex protective oxides (e.g., spinels) can reduce oxygen-driven surface degradation (PMC7515071). Most recently, investigations into WVTaTiCr coatings on steel revealed that higher Cr content promotes a continuous, protective oxide layer, leading to improved high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance (PMC10142552). Although these works underscore the importance of stable surface scales and/or passivation layers to limit oxygen penetration, they also highlight challenges in forming uniform, adherent protective layers without compromising mechanical performance, especially under extreme thermal and mechanical loads.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress in incorporating oxide-forming elements directly into the bulk composition, the community still seeks robust, scalable strategies to create stable, adherent, and protective oxide layers in refractory HEAs under very high temperatures and highly oxidizing conditions. Moreover, it remains unclear which specific modification strategies (beyond simply adding alloying elements) can reliably yield improved oxidation resistance without sacrificing mechanical properties or introducing major cost or fabrication challenges.
decision.lever: A single-step, high-temperature pre-oxidation treatment in a controlled low-pressure oxygen atmosphere to grow a dense, protective oxide layer on exposed surfaces
decision.why: Building on prior results that emphasize the efficacy of stable surface oxides (e.g., spinels or chromia) in preventing rapid oxygen ingress, a dedicated pre-oxidation step can induce uniform scale development without altering bulk alloy chemistry. The literature (PMC7515071, PMC10142552) has shown that an initially formed oxide can dramatically improve resistance to further oxidation at high temperatures, but achieving sufficient adherence and uniformity remains a challenge that this controlled treatment intends to address. By tuning factors such as temperature (e.g., 1000–1200 °C), duration (1–2 hours), and a carefully chosen low partial pressure of oxygen (10⁻³–10⁻⁵ atm), the alloy surface can reliably form a passivating oxide scale, which is expected to maintain structural integrity longer than an untreated surface. To test this hypothesis, one can subject both pre-oxidized and untreated specimens of the same refractory HEA to a 1200 °C cyclic-oxidation environment in air for 200 hours, measuring spallation mass loss and oxygen diffusion depth. If the pre-oxidized samples do not show a lower mass gain and shallower oxygen penetration than the untreated controls, or if their protective scale spalls off significantly, the hypothesis would be falsified.
